claim: Hevin is an astrocyte-secreted extracellular matrix protein that localizes to the clefts of excitatory synapses.
source: For example, hevin (a.k.a. synaptic cleft-1 or SPARC-like 1) is an astrocyte-secreted extracellular matrix protein that localizes to the clefts of excitatory synapses (Johnston et al., 1990; Lively et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Johnston et al., 1990 and Lively et al., 2007

claim: Hevin promotes excitatory synaptogenesis.
source: For example, hevin (a.k.a. synaptic cleft-1 or SPARC-like 1) is an astrocyte-secreted extracellular matrix protein that localizes to the clefts of excitatory synapses (Johnston et al., 1990; Lively et al., 2007) and promotes excitatory synaptogenesis (Kucukdereli et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kucukdereli et al., 2011

claim: Hevin expression is largely restricted to astrocytes in the cortex.
source: Staining for cell-specific markers confirms that hevin expression is largely restricted to astrocytes in the cortex (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1C-E

claim: Hevin expression in the cortex peaks during P15-P25.
source: Hevin is expressed throughout the cortex in a developmentally regulated manner, peaking during P15–P25, a time period that coincides with intense synapse formation, maturation and elimination events in the cortex (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: The number of VGlut1+ intracortical synapses in the S/Z of hevin KOs were significantly higher when compared to littermate WTs at P25.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the number of VGlut1+ intracortical synapses in the S/Z of hevin KOs were significantly higher when compared to littermate WTs at P25 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Thalamocortical VGlut2+ synapses were profoundly reduced in hevin KOs compared to WTs at P25.
source: In contrast, thalamocortical VGlut2+ synapses were profoundly reduced in hevin KOs compared to WTs at P25 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Neuronal density and layering was similar between P25 WT and hevin KO.
source: The severe loss of thalamocortical synapses in hevin KOs was not due to a gross cellular defect in hevin KO cortices, because we found that neuronal density and layering was similar between P25 WT and hevin KO (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by NeuN staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: There was a significant reduction in VGlut2+ synaptic terminals across multiple cortical layers in the hevin KOs.
source: However, we observed a significant reduction in VGlut2+ synaptic terminals across multiple cortical layers in the hevin KOs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by VGlut2 staining intensity data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: Lack of hevin did not impair the ability of thalamic projections to reach the S/Z.
source: Moreover, by using a viral approach to trace the thalamic axons that project to V1 cortex, we found that lack of hevin did not impair the ability of thalamic projections to reach the S/Z (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by viral tracing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B-D

claim: P7 hevin KO cortex showed a severe deficit in VGlut2+ synapses.
source: However, similar to P25, P7 hevin KO cortex showed a severe deficit in VGlut2+ synapses (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification data shown in Figure 3C

claim: VGlut2+ synapse density was still significantly lower in the 12-week old hevin KO adults compared to WT.
source: The specific loss of thalamocortical synaptic connectivity in hevin KOs was not merely a developmental delay in thalamocortical synaptogenesis, since VGlut2+ synapse density was still significantly lower in the 12-week old hevin KO adults compared to WT (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The number of VGlut1+ synapses in the hevin KOs returned to normal levels in the adult.
source: However, the number of VGlut1+ synapses in the hevin KOs returned to normal levels in the adult (Figure 3D)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Recordings from P23–P26 mice did not show any significant differences in miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons of hevin KOs when compared to their littermate WTs.
source: In agreement with this possibility, recordings from P23–P26 mice did not show any significant differences in miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons of hevin KOs when compared to their littermate WTs (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: Hevin treatment did not increase the number of VGlut1+ synaptic puncta in either the cortical neuron only cultures or in the cortical/thalamic neuron co-cultures.
source: Hevin treatment did not increase the number of VGlut1+ synaptic puncta (determined as the co-localization of VGlut1 and PSD95) in either the cortical neuron only cultures or in the cortical/thalamic neuron co-cultures (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro synapse quantification data shown in Figure 4B,C

claim: Hevin treatment significantly increased VGlut2+ synapse formation onto cortical neurons in cortical-thalamic co-cultures.
source: However, hevin treatment significantly increased VGlut2+ synapse formation onto cortical neurons in cortical-thalamic co-cultures (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro synapse quantification data shown in Figure 4D,E

claim: Hevin-injected cortices showed a robust increase in VGlut2+ thalamocortical terminal staining throughout the S/Z and Layer II/III directly adjacent to the site of injection.
source: Compared to vehicle-injected littermate controls, hevin-injected cortices showed a robust increase in VGlut2+ thalamocortical terminal staining throughout the S/Z and Layer II/III directly adjacent to the site of injection (Figure 4F, asterisk and arrow, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo hevin injection data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Quantitative analysis of co-localized VGlut2/PSD95 synaptic puncta in the S/Z revealed a significant increase in thalamocortical synapses in hevin-injected cortices compared to the vehicle-injected littermates.
source: Quantitative analysis of co-localized VGlut2/PSD95 synaptic puncta in the S/Z also revealed a significant increase in thalamocortical synapses in hevin-injected cortices compared to the vehicle-injected littermates (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo synapse quantification data shown in Figure 4G,H

claim: The number of co-localized VGlut1/PSD95 synaptic puncta was not affected by hevin injection.
source: By contrast, the number of co-localized VGlut1/PSD95 synaptic puncta was not affected by hevin injection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo synapse quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Analyses of spines in V1 of littermate hevin KO and WT mice at P25 by Golgi-Cox staining showed a significant increase in immature filopodia-like protrusions in P25 hevin KOs concomitant with a decrease in mature mushroom spines compared to littermate WT controls.
source: Analyses of spines in V1 of littermate hevin KO and WT mice at P25 by Golgi-Cox staining showed a significant increase in immature filopodia-like protrusions in P25 hevin KOs concomitant with a decrease in mature mushroom spines compared to littermate WT controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Golgi-Cox staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: There was no significant difference in total protrusion density between genotypes.
source: There was no significant difference in total protrusion density between genotypes (WT, 1.12 ± 0.03 spines/µm; KO, 1.07 ± 0.03 spines/µm; n = 45 dendrites per condition; p > 0.05, Student's t test).
evidence: The claim is supported by Golgi-Cox staining quantification data

claim: The dendritic arborization of layer II/III neurons was similar between hevin KO and WT mice.
source: The dendritic arborization of layer II/III neurons was also similar between hevin KO and WT mice, showing that lack of hevin does not lead to overt problems in dendritic morphology (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Analysis of postsynaptic density (PSD) area revealed smaller, asymmetric (i.e., excitatory) synapse area in hevin KO V1.
source: Analysis of postsynaptic density (PSD) area revealed smaller, asymmetric (i.e., excitatory) synapse area in hevin KO V1 (Figure 5B), indicative of synaptic immaturity.
evidence: The claim is supported by serial section electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Overall asymmetric synapse density was not significantly affected in hevin KO V1.
source: Despite the deficits in synapse morphology, overall asymmetric synapse density was not significantly affected in hevin KO V1 (WT, 2.16 ± 0.16 synapses/µm; KO, 2.63 ± 0.27 synapses/µm; n = 12 dendrites per condition; p = 0.15, Student's t test).
evidence: The claim is supported by serial section electron microscopy quantification data

claim: No difference in astrocyte contact was found between WT and hevin KO synapses.
source: Since hevin is primarily expressed and secreted by astrocytes, we postulated that hevin KOs may have altered astroglial contact at synapses, but no difference in astrocyte contact was found between WT and hevin KO synapses (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5C

claim: A fraction of excitatory synapses in the hevin KOs was made directly onto the dendritic shafts rather than on spines.
source: Interestingly, a fraction of excitatory synapses in the hevin KOs was made directly onto the dendritic shafts rather than on spines (Figure 5D), a configuration that was rare in the WTs at P25.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5D

claim: SMEC density was significantly higher in P25 hevin KO mice compared to WT.
source: SMEC density was significantly higher in P25 hevin KO mice compared to WT (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by serial section electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5E

claim: 25% of all excitatory connections are formed onto SMECs at P14.
source: Remarkably, 25% of all excitatory connections are formed onto SMECs at P14, a finding that may have gone unnoticed if not for the spatial resolution offered by 3D ssEM.
evidence: The claim is supported by serial section electron microscopy quantification data

claim: The prevalence of SMECs is largely decreased by P25.
source: The prevalence of SMECs is largely decreased by P25 (Figure 6C,D), indicating that SMECs represent a transient stage in excitatory synaptic maturation.
evidence: The claim is supported by serial section electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6C,D

claim: If an axon made a connection with a SMEC, it had nearly a 50% chance of contacting another SMEC nearby.
source: We found that if an axon made a connection with a SMEC, it had nearly a 50% chance of contacting another SMEC nearby (42.5% in P14 WT, 45.4% in P25 WT, 41.6% in P25 hevin KO; Figure 7A, Video 1), which is vastly higher than what would be expected by chance (6.4% in P14 WT, 0.5% in P25 WT, 3.1% in P25 hevin KO).
evidence: The claim is supported by serial section electron microscopy axon reconstruction data shown in Figure 7A

claim: A SMEC can receive simultaneous cortical (VGlut1+) and thalamic (VGlut2+) inputs.
source: To provide evidence for this possibility, we next performed immuno-EM analysis using VGlut1 and VGlut2-specific antibodies on conventional 2D-EM sections from P14 WT mice and observed that a SMEC can indeed receive simultaneous cortical (VGlut1+) and thalamic (VGlut2+) inputs (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immuno-EM data shown in Figure 7B

claim: 10.97% of VGlut terminals appeared to co-localize in P15 WT, which was significantly reduced in P25 WT.
source: We found that, in agreement with earlier findings from other brain regions and layers (Herzog et al., 2006; Nakamura et al., 2007), 10.97% of VGlut terminals appeared to co-localize in P15 WT, which was significantly reduced in P25 WT (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B and citations to Herzog et al., 2006 and Nakamura et al., 2007

claim: The frequency of overlap in the P25 hevin KO was essentially unchanged compared to P15 and was significantly higher than the P25 WT.
source: Interestingly, the frequency of overlap in the P25 hevin KO was essentially unchanged compared to P15 and was significantly higher than the P25 WT (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: SIM imaging of VGlut1 and VGlut2 puncta in P15 WT showed virtually no co-localized presynaptic puncta.
source: Indeed, SIM imaging of VGlut1 and VGlut2 puncta in P15 WT showed virtually no co-localized presynaptic puncta (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structured illumination microscopy data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D

claim: The majority of SMECs were innervated by both VGlut1 and VGlut2 inputs at P15.
source: In accordance with a role for SMECs in synaptic competition during development, the majority of SMECs were innervated by both VGlut1 and VGlut2 inputs at this age, with fewer examples of VGlut1/VGlut1 and VGlut2/VGlut2 SMECs (Figure 8—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in utero electroporation and confocal imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2E

claim: The majority of SMECs in P21 hevin KO received mixed VGlut1/VGlut2 inputs.
source: In addition to confirming the overall increase in SMECs in the hevin KO, the 3D reconstructions revealed that the majority of these SMECs indeed received mixed VGlut1/VGlut2 inputs (Figure 8A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by in utero electroporation and confocal imaging data shown in Figure 8A,B

claim: Intracortical and thalamocortical connections can be distinguished as they primarily contain either vesicular glutamate transporter-1 (VGlut1) or VGlut2 in their presynaptic terminals, respectively.
source: Intracortical and thalamocortical connections can be distinguished as they primarily contain either vesicular glutamate transporter-1 (VGlut1) or VGlut2 in their presynaptic terminals, respectively (Kaneko and Fujiyama, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kaneko and Fujiyama, 2002

claim: In most cortical areas, VGlut1-positive (VGlut1+) intracortical projections greatly outnumber the VGlut2+ thalamic projections.
source: In most cortical areas, VGlut1-positive (VGlut1+) intracortical projections greatly outnumber the VGlut2+ thalamic projections.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cortical connectivity

claim: Innervation of the cortex by projecting neurites called axons begins during embryonic development and continues for the first several postnatal days.
source: In the mouse brain, innervation of the cortex by projecting neurites called axons begins during embryonic development and continues for the first several postnatal days (Garel and Lopez-Bendito, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Garel and Lopez-Bendito, 2014

claim: An intense period of synapse formation occurs during the second and third postnatal weeks in mice.
source: Only after the axons project to their approximate target areas, hosting their suitable postsynaptic partners, does an intense period of synapse formation occur, corresponding roughly to the second and third postnatal weeks in mice (Li et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2010

claim: Cortical excitatory synapses are formed between dendritic protrusions called spines and axonal projections coming from two predominant inputs: intracortical and thalamic.
source: Cortical excitatory synapses, which primarily use the neurotransmitter glutamate, are formed between dendritic protrusions called spines and axonal projections coming from two predominant inputs: intracortical and thalamic.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cortical synaptic organization

claim: The bulk of the cortical synapses from both intracortical and thalamic inputs are made during the same early postnatal synaptogenic period (P5–P21).
source: Though the bulk of the cortical synapses from both of these inputs are made during the same early postnatal synaptogenic period (P5–P21) (Nakamura et al., 2005), whether they form through similar or differential mechanisms is unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2005

claim: Astrocytes begin to populate the cortex during the synaptogenic period, producing and secreting factors that promote synaptogenesis.
source: Concurrently with the synaptogenic period, non-neuronal cells called astrocytes begin to populate the cortex, producing and secreting factors that promote synaptogenesis (Eroglu and Barres, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Eroglu and Barres, 2010

claim: Hevin is required for the correct formation and maturation of RGC synapses onto their postsynaptic target, the superior colliculus.
source: The astrocyte-secreted synaptogenic protein hevin (a.k.a. SPARC-like 1/SPARCL-1 or Synaptic Cleft-1/SC1) increases the number of synapses made between retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) in vitro and is required for the correct formation and maturation of RGC synapses onto their postsynaptic target, the superior colliculus (Kucukdereli et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kucukdereli et al., 2011

claim: Multiply-innervated spines were identified nearly a half-century ago by Jones and Powell.
source: Multiply-innervated spines were identified nearly a half-century ago by Jones and Powell (1969).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jones and Powell, 1969

claim: The majority of multiply-innervated spines make two distinct types of synapses: one excitatory with an asymmetric postsynaptic density (PSD) opposed to an axon with round presynaptic vesicles, and one inhibitory synapse with a symmetrical PSD and flattened vesicles.
source: The majority of these spines make two distinct types of synapses: one excitatory with an asymmetric postsynaptic density (PSD) opposed to an axon with round presynaptic vesicles, and one inhibitory synapse with a symmetrical PSD and flattened vesicles (Jones and Powell, 1969; Knott et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jones and Powell, 1969; Knott et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2012

claim: During development, spontaneous retinal activity relayed by thalamus facilitates proper patterning and connectivity within visual cortex.
source: During development, spontaneous retinal activity relayed by thalamus facilitates proper patterning and connectivity within visual cortex (Ackman and Crair, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ackman and Crair, 2014

claim: Perturbations in synaptic competition for eye-specific territories in V1 can compromise dendritic spine refinement.
source: Furthermore, it was previously shown that perturbations in synaptic competition for eye-specific territories in V1 can compromise dendritic spine refinement (Mataga et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mataga et al., 2004

claim: Excitatory shaft synapses are among the first synapses to form along dendrites.
source: It is postulated that excitatory shaft synapses are among the first synapses to form along dendrites (Reilly et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Reilly et al., 2011

claim: Shaft synapses may be induced to become spines by presynaptic activity during the early stages of postnatal development (P8–P12).
source: These shaft synapses may be induced to become spines by presynaptic activity during the early stages of postnatal development (P8–P12) (Kwon and Sabatini, 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kwon and Sabatini, 2011

claim: Hevin has been known to modulate cell adhesion.
source: Hevin has been known to modulate cell adhesion (Sullivan and Sage, 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sullivan and Sage, 2004

claim: Multiply-innervated filopodia have been seen in the juvenile CA1 region of hippocampus.
source: In agreement with this, multiply-innervated filopodia have been seen in the juvenile CA1 region of hippocampus (Fiala et al., 1998)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fiala et al., 1998

claim: Live imaging of green fluorescent protein (GFP)-labeled dendrites in acute hippocampal slices from P10–12 mice showed that spines sample nearby synaptic resources even after making a stable contact.
source: In addition, live imaging of green fluorescent protein (GFP)-labeled dendrites in acute hippocampal slices from P10–12 mice showed that spines sample nearby synaptic resources even after making a stable contact (Konur and Yuste, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Konur and Yuste, 2004

claim: Hevin is strongly upregulated in reactive astrocytes in disease conditions.
source: Hevin is strongly upregulated in reactive astrocytes in disease conditions (McKinnon and Margolskee, 1996)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McKinnon and Margolskee, 1996

claim: Hevin has been linked to neurological disorders, including autism, schizophrenia, suicide and depression.
source: Hevin is strongly upregulated in reactive astrocytes in disease conditions (McKinnon and Margolskee, 1996) and has also been linked to neurological disorders, including autism, schizophrenia, suicide and depression (Purcell et al., 2001; Jacquemont et al., 2006; Kahler et al., 2008; Vialou et al., 2010; Zhurov et al., 2012; De Rubeis et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Purcell et al., 2001; Jacquemont et al., 2006; Kahler et al., 2008; Vialou et al., 2010; Zhurov et al., 2012; De Rubeis et al., 2014

claim: Abnormal spine maturation and connectivity have been observed in autism, schizophrenia, suicide, depression and other diseases.
source: Abnormal spine maturation and connectivity have also been observed in these and other diseases (Fiala et al., 2002; De Rubeis et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fiala et al., 2002; De Rubeis et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2013

claim: SMEC-like 'giant spines' have been observed in hippocampi from patients with severe temporal lobe epilepsy.
source: Abnormal spine maturation and connectivity have also been observed in these and other diseases (Fiala et al., 2002; De Rubeis et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2013), including the presence of SMEC-like 'giant spines' in hippocampi from patients with severe temporal lobe epilepsy (Witcher et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Witcher et al., 2010

claim: Astrocyte-secreted protein hevin is required for normal thalamocortical synaptic connectivity in the mouse cortex.
source: Here, we show that astrocyte-secreted protein hevin is required for normal thalamocortical synaptic connectivity in the mouse cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript including immunohistochemistry, in vitro assays, and in vivo injections

claim: Absence of hevin results in a profound, long-lasting reduction in thalamocortical synapses accompanied by a transient increase in intracortical excitatory connections.
source: Absence of hevin results in a profound, long-lasting reduction in thalamocortical synapses accompanied by a transient increase in intracortical excitatory connections.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data at multiple developmental time points (P7, P25, adult)

claim: During early postnatal development, dendritic spines often receive multiple excitatory inputs.
source: Three-dimensional reconstructions of cortical neurons from serial section electron microscopy (ssEM) revealed that, during early postnatal development, dendritic spines often receive multiple excitatory inputs.
evidence: The claim is supported by serial section electron microscopy data

claim: Majority of the spines with multiple excitatory contacts (SMECs) receive simultaneous thalamic and cortical inputs.
source: Immuno-EM and confocal analyses revealed that majority of the spines with multiple excitatory contacts (SMECs) receive simultaneous thalamic and cortical inputs.
evidence: The claim is supported by immuno-EM and confocal imaging data

claim: Proportion of SMECs diminishes as the brain develops.
source: Proportion of SMECs diminishes as the brain develops, but SMECs remain abundant in Hevin-null mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by serial section electron microscopy data comparing P14 and P25 WT mice

claim: SMECs remain abundant in Hevin-null mice.
source: Proportion of SMECs diminishes as the brain develops, but SMECs remain abundant in Hevin-null mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by serial section electron microscopy data comparing P25 WT and hevin KO mice

claim: Through secretion of hevin, astrocytes control an important developmental synaptic refinement process at dendritic spines.
source: These findings reveal that, through secretion of hevin, astrocytes control an important developmental synaptic refinement process at dendritic spines.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined experimental data showing hevin's role in SMEC resolution and thalamocortical synapse formation

claim: During cortical synaptic development, dendritic spines serve as sites of competition between thalamic and cortical axons.
source: These results suggest that, during cortical synaptic development, dendritic spines serve as sites of competition between thalamic and cortical axons.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the finding that SMECs receive simultaneous VGlut1 and VGlut2 inputs

claim: Through secretion of hevin, astrocytes help maintain thalamic inputs onto cortical neurons and facilitate resolution of SMECs into singly-innervated spines.
source: Through secretion of hevin, astrocytes help maintain thalamic inputs onto cortical neurons and facilitate resolution of SMECs into singly-innervated spines.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined findings that hevin is required for thalamocortical synapses and that SMECs persist in hevin KO mice

claim: In the developing visual cortex, SMECs serve as sites at which cortical and thalamic inputs compete.
source: Based on our findings, we propose that, in the developing visual cortex, SMECs serve as sites at which cortical and thalamic inputs compete (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the experimental findings

claim: This competition is normally resolved by P25 with the establishment of single synapse spines contacting either VGlut1+ or VGlut2+ terminals.
source: This competition is normally resolved by P25 with the establishment of single synapse spines contacting either VGlut1+ or VGlut2+ terminals.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the developmental time course of SMEC prevalence

claim: This resolution is dependent on astrocyte-secreted hevin to stabilize VGlut2+ synapses.
source: This resolution is dependent on astrocyte-secreted hevin to stabilize VGlut2+ synapses.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the persistence of SMECs and loss of VGlut2 synapses in hevin KO mice

claim: In the absence of hevin, the VGlut2+ connections cannot be stabilized thus cannot effectively compete with VGlut1+ terminals for postsynaptic spines, resulting in increased VGlut1+ synapses and the persistence of SMECs.
source: In the absence of hevin, the VGlut2+ connections cannot be stabilized thus cannot effectively compete with VGlut1+ terminals for postsynaptic spines, resulting in increased VGlut1+ synapses and the persistence of SMECs (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the experimental findings in hevin KO mice

claim: The reduction in VGlut2+ synapses in hevin KO V1 enable synaptic takeover by the more abundant VGlut1+ projections.
source: Our findings also suggest that the reduction in VGlut2+ synapses in hevin KO V1 enable synaptic takeover by the more abundant VGlut1+ projections.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed increase in VGlut1 synapses when VGlut2 synapses are reduced

claim: Retraction of one axon is often succeeded by the expansion of another.
source: In agreement with this possibility, previous observations of synaptic competition have shown that retraction of one axon is often succeeded by the expansion of another (Walsh and Lichtman, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Walsh and Lichtman, 2003

claim: Defective thalamocortical connectivity in hevin KO mice may be responsible for driving generalized spine synapse immaturity in the cortex.
source: Defective thalamocortical connectivity in hevin KO mice may therefore be responsible for driving generalized spine synapse immaturity in the cortex.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the observed spine immaturity in hevin KO mice

claim: Hevin may act as a 'protection signal' to prevent elimination of thalamocortical synapses.
source: Hevin may also act as a 'protection signal' (Sanes and Lichtman, 1999) to prevent elimination of thalamocortical synapses.
evidence: The claim is speculation about hevin's mechanism of action, with citation to Sanes and Lichtman, 1999

claim: VGlut1+ intracortical synapses may have redundant stabilization/protection mechanisms in place that can compensate for the lack of hevin.
source: Alternatively, hevin is a generalized protective signal but VGlut1+ intracortical synapses may have redundant stabilization/protection mechanisms in place that can compensate for the lack of hevin, whereas with no such compensation available the VGlut2+ thalamocortical population is lost.
evidence: The claim is speculation about potential compensatory mechanisms

claim: There may be specific hevin interactors present on thalamocortical synapses that distinguish them from the intracortical ones.
source: Because hevin is preferentially inducing thalamocortical synapses, there may be specific hevin interactors present on these synapses that distinguish them from the intracortical ones.
evidence: The claim is speculation about potential molecular mechanisms

claim: Thalamocortical connectivity in general and/or hevin in particular may be playing a role in the shaft to spine transition of some synapses.
source: These shaft synapses may be induced to become spines by presynaptic activity during the early stages of postnatal development (P8–P12) (Kwon and Sabatini, 2011); our results suggest that thalamocortical connectivity in general and/or hevin in particular may be playing a role in the shaft to spine transition of some synapses.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the observed increase in shaft synapses in hevin KO mice, with citation to Kwon and Sabatini, 2011

claim: Impaired resolution of axonal competition by astrocytes may drive the dendritic spine deficiencies observed in neurological disorders.
source: Future studies may determine if impaired resolution of axonal competition by astrocytes drives the dendritic spine deficiencies observed in these conditions, providing a novel cellular target for therapeutic strategies.
evidence: The claim is speculation about potential clinical implications
